outOfScope: choosing WIP limits for a real team

claims.claim: Kanban is a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process, using defined and visualized workflow, active management, and improvement.
A Definition of Workflow includes work items, start and finish points, states, WIP control, and explicit movement policies; a Kanban board visualizes that definition.
Controlling WIP can create a pull system in which a new item is selected when there is a clear signal of capacity.
The minimum Kanban flow metrics are WIP, throughput, work item age, and cycle time, each defined differently.
Scrum is a distinct framework with defined accountabilities and time-bounded Sprints, so these are not minimum Kanban requirements.
Flow measurements need context and are useful when they inform workflow practices; they do not alone guarantee future outcomes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Kanban terminology and practices can be described differently across communities, while this lesson needs a bounded general-education definition.
positions: The Kanban Guide presents a minimal, current reference for Kanban in knowledge work.
Many commercial and practitioner sources describe boards, methods, or organizational implementations with additional conventions.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the Guide for core definitions, avoids claiming a universal board design or a prescribed WIP value, and frames examples as hypothetical.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic and had no source-backed account of Kanban, WIP control, flow metrics, or its distinction from Scrum.
correctionsNeeded: Replace boilerplate with a source-verified description of visualized workflow, pull, WIP, and the four flow metrics.
Distinguish Kanban from Scrum rather than treating either name as a general synonym for a task board.
Keep examples illustrative and exclude implementation, staffing, prioritization, and organization-specific advice.
rightsIssues: The Kanban Guide and Scrum Guide are used as reference-only sources. The lesson uses original prose and does not reproduce source text, diagrams, templates, or framework materials.
